content.name: p
children: Webhooks are how one system notifies another system of a state change.

content.name: p
children: In architectural terms, a webhook is a programming language agnostic approach for sending messages between distributed systems. The power of webhooks comes first from being independent of any specific tech stack and second from the notification-based approach. Regardless of your architecture, your systems can receive or broadcast webhooks without being dependent on a specific vendor or even on the same network. Further, downstream systems receiving webhooks don't need to poll a central system for updates or status changes, they can simply listen for an event and process the results.

content.name: p
children: In practical terms, a webhook is simply an HTTP request - usually a POST or GET - with a JSON payload or parameters broadcast from the central system. Much of the modern web is built on this distributed communication pattern. They're popularly used to notify third-party systems of events such as a new incident tracked by PagerDuty, a successful payment in
, or a pull request opened on

content.name: p
children: Without webhooks, a system that needs to know about changes has to poll: call an API every few seconds or minutes and compare the results. Polling wastes requests when nothing changed and adds delay when something did. Webhooks flip the direction — the provider sends a request when the event happens. The trade-off is that the consumer must run a public endpoint, verify that requests are genuine, and cope with failed and repeated deliveries.

content.name: p
children: A typical webhook delivery looks like this:
